lessons.title: What Are Mobile Apps
lessons.content: A mobile app is software designed to run on smartphones and tablets. Native apps are built for one platform (Android with Kotlin/Java, iOS with Swift) — they're fast and can use all device features. Cross-platform apps (Flutter, React Native) use one codebase for both platforms — faster to develop. Web apps run in a browser and work everywhere but can't access all device features. Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) are web apps that can be installed and work offline. When choosing your approach, consider: target audience, budget, features needed, and development speed.
examples: Instagram is a native app — separate code for Android and iOS
Flutter lets you write one Dart codebase that runs on Android, iOS, Windows, and web
Twitter has a PWA — you can install it from the browser and it works offline

keyTerms.native app: An app built specifically for one platform using its native language
keyTerms.cross-platform: Building one app that works on multiple platforms (Android, iOS, web)
keyTerms.PWA: Progressive Web App — a web app that can be installed and works offline

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of cross-platform development?
quiz.explanation: Cross-platform means writing code once and deploying to Android, iOS, and more.

quiz.question: Which language is used for native Android development?
quiz.explanation: Kotlin (and Java) are the native languages for Android app development.

quiz.question: What makes a PWA different from a regular website?
options: It can be installed and works offline
It requires a download from app stores
quiz.explanation: PWAs can be installed on the home screen and cache content for offline use.

lessons.title: UI/UX Design Principles
lessons.content: UI (User Interface) is what the app looks like — buttons, colors, text, icons. UX (User Experience) is how it feels to use — is it easy, intuitive, frustrating? Good UX follows principles: consistency (same patterns throughout), feedback (the app responds to every action), simplicity (don't overwhelm users), accessibility (usable by people with disabilities). The navigation should be obvious — users shouldn't need instructions. Use established patterns: bottom navigation bars, pull to refresh, swipe gestures. Always test with real users to find problems you missed.
examples: A loading spinner gives feedback — the user knows something is happening
Bottom navigation bar (Home, Search, Profile) is a pattern users already understand
High contrast text (dark on light) ensures readability for all users including those with visual impairments

keyTerms.UI: User Interface — the visual design elements users see and interact with
keyTerms.UX: User Experience — how easy and pleasant an app is to use overall
keyTerms.accessibility: Designing apps usable by people with disabilities (screen readers, color contrast)

quiz.question: What is the difference between UI and UX?
options: UI is how it looks, UX is how it feels to use
UI is backend, UX is frontend
UI is for mobile, UX is for web
quiz.explanation: UI = visual design (buttons, colors), UX = the overall experience (ease, satisfaction).

quiz.question: Why is consistency important in app design?
options: Users learn patterns once and apply them everywhere
It makes the app look boring
It reduces the number of screens
quiz.explanation: Consistent design means users don't have to relearn how things work on each screen.

quiz.question: What does accessibility mean in app design?
quiz.explanation: Accessibility ensures everyone can use the app, including people with visual, hearing, or motor impairments.

lessons.title: App Architecture Patterns
lessons.content: Architecture is how you organize your app's code. MVC (Model-View-Controller): Model holds data, View displays it, Controller handles logic. MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel): the ViewModel prepares data for the View and handles user actions — popular in modern apps. Clean Architecture separates code into layers: presentation (UI), domain (business logic), and data (databases, APIs). State management is crucial — it tracks what the app is showing and what data is loaded. Good architecture makes apps easier to test, debug, and extend. Separation of concerns means each part does one job.
examples: View: the login screen with email/password fields and a button
Model: the User object with name, email, and profile picture data
ViewModel: takes user input, validates it, calls the login API, and tells the View the result

keyTerms.MVC: Model-View-Controller — a pattern separating data, display, and logic
keyTerms.state management: Tracking and updating what the app is currently displaying
keyTerms.separation of concerns: Each code module handles one responsibility only

quiz.question: In MVC, what does the View do?
quiz.explanation: The View is the UI layer — it shows data to the user.

quiz.question: Why is state management important?
options: It tracks what the app should display at any moment
quiz.explanation: State management ensures the UI always reflects the current data and user actions.

quiz.question: What is separation of concerns?
options: Each part of code handles one specific responsibility
quiz.explanation: Each module does one job — UI code doesn't mix with data logic.

lessons.title: Widgets and Components
lessons.content: In modern app frameworks, everything on screen is a widget (Flutter) or component (React Native). A widget is a reusable UI building block — a button, text field, image, or card. Widgets nest inside each other to build complex layouts: a Screen contains a Column, which contains a Card, which contains Text and an Image. Widgets can be stateless (display fixed content) or stateful (change based on user interaction). Building apps means composing small widgets into larger ones — like LEGO blocks.
examples: A Text widget displays a string: Text('Hello World')
A Column widget arranges children vertically: Column(children: [Text('Title'), Text('Subtitle')])
A Button widget responds to taps: ElevatedButton(onPressed: login, child: Text('Log In'))

keyTerms.widget: A reusable UI building block that describes part of the interface
keyTerms.stateless: A widget that doesn't change — its content is fixed once built
keyTerms.stateful: A widget that can change its appearance based on user interaction or data

quiz.question: What is a widget?
quiz.explanation: Widgets are the fundamental building blocks of app interfaces.

quiz.question: When would you use a stateful widget?
options: When the UI needs to change based on user action
quiz.explanation: Stateful widgets rebuild when their internal state changes (toggles, counters, forms).

quiz.question: How do you create complex layouts?
quiz.explanation: Complex UIs are built by composing smaller widgets into larger structures.

lessons.title: Layouts and Navigation
lessons.content: Layout determines how widgets are arranged on screen. Row arranges children horizontally. Column arranges vertically. Stack layers widgets on top of each other. ListView creates scrollable lists. GridView creates scrollable grids. Navigation moves users between screens. Common patterns: bottom navigation bar (3-5 main tabs), drawer menu (hamburger menu for more options), and stack navigation (push/pop screens like a deck of cards). Deep linking lets users open specific screens directly from a URL or notification.
examples: Row(children: [Icon(star), Text('Favorite')]) — icon and text side by side
Navigator.push(context, MaterialPageRoute(builder: (_) => DetailScreen())) — opens a new screen
BottomNavigationBar with Home, Search, and Profile tabs — tap to switch sections

keyTerms.Row: A layout widget that arranges children in a horizontal line
keyTerms.Column: A layout widget that arranges children in a vertical line
keyTerms.navigation: Moving between different screens or pages in an app

quiz.question: Which layout arranges items vertically?
quiz.explanation: Column arranges children from top to bottom (vertically).

quiz.question: What is a bottom navigation bar used for?
quiz.explanation: Bottom nav bars provide quick access to 3-5 main sections of the app.

quiz.question: Stack navigation works like:
options: A deck of cards — push new screens on top, pop to go back
quiz.explanation: Push adds a screen on top; pop removes it, revealing the previous one.

lessons.title: Handling User Input
lessons.content: Apps need to capture and respond to user input. Text fields collect typed text — validate input (is the email valid? is the password strong enough?). Buttons trigger actions on tap. Gesture detectors handle swipes, long presses, and drags. Forms group multiple inputs together and validate them all at once before submitting. Show feedback: loading indicators while processing, success messages, error states with clear explanations. Handle keyboard interactions — show/hide the keyboard appropriately, don't let it cover input fields.
examples: TextField with validation: if email doesn't contain @, show 'Invalid email'
A form with name, email, and message fields — validate all before sending
Show a SnackBar after saving: 'Profile updated successfully!'

keyTerms.validation: Checking that user input meets required criteria before processing
keyTerms.gesture: A touch interaction like tap, swipe, long press, or pinch
keyTerms.form: A group of input fields that can be validated and submitted together

quiz.question: Why validate user input?
options: To ensure data is correct before processing
quiz.explanation: Validation catches errors early — preventing crashes and ensuring data quality.

quiz.question: What is a gesture in app development?
options: A touch interaction like tap or swipe
quiz.explanation: Gestures are touch-based interactions: tap, double tap, swipe, long press, pinch.

quiz.question: What should you show while data is loading?
quiz.explanation: A spinner or progress bar tells the user something is happening — don't leave them guessing.

lessons.title: Local Data Storage
lessons.content: Apps store data locally on the device. SharedPreferences/UserDefaults store simple key-value pairs (settings, user preferences). SQLite is a lightweight database for structured data (user profiles, saved items, history). File storage saves files to the device (downloaded images, exported data). Choose the right tool: settings → key-value, structured records → SQLite, large files → file system. Always handle the case where data doesn't exist yet (first app launch). Consider data size and performance — don't store large files in SQLite.
examples: SharedPreferences: save theme preference as isDarkMode = true
SQLite: store student profiles with name, age, grade, and learning history
File storage: save a generated PDF certificate to the device's documents folder

keyTerms.SharedPreferences: Simple key-value storage for small data like settings and preferences
keyTerms.SQLite: A lightweight local database for structured data with tables and queries
keyTerms.local storage: Storing data on the device itself, available offline

quiz.question: Where should you store a user's theme preference?
quiz.explanation: Simple settings like theme preference are perfect for key-value storage.

quiz.question: When would you use SQLite?
options: For structured data with multiple records (like a contact list)
quiz.explanation: SQLite handles structured data with tables, rows, and queries — ideal for lists and records.

quiz.question: Why is local storage important?
quiz.explanation: Local storage is offline-capable, fast, and doesn't require server costs.

lessons.title: State Management
lessons.content: State is the data your app is currently using — which screen is shown, is the user logged in, what items are in the cart. Local state belongs to one widget (a text field's current value). Global state is shared across the app (user profile, theme, cart). State management solutions: setState (simple, local), Provider/Riverpod (medium complexity, recommended), BLoC (complex, enterprise). The key principle: when state changes, the UI automatically rebuilds to reflect it. One-way data flow keeps things predictable: user action → state update → UI rebuild.
examples: Local state: a counter widget tracks its own count with setState
Global state: the logged-in user's profile is available on every screen via a Provider
When the user adds an item to cart, the cart icon badge updates automatically across the app

keyTerms.state: The current data and conditions of the app at any moment
keyTerms.Provider: A state management solution that makes data available throughout the widget tree
keyTerms.reactive: The UI automatically updates whenever the underlying state changes

quiz.question: What is 'state' in an app?
options: The current data and conditions the app is using
quiz.explanation: State includes everything the app currently knows: user data, screen, settings, etc.

quiz.question: When should you use global state instead of local state?
options: When data needs to be shared across multiple screens
quiz.explanation: Global state is for data needed in multiple places — user profile, theme, cart.

quiz.question: In reactive state management, when state changes:
quiz.explanation: Reactive means the UI watches the state and rebuilds whenever it changes.

lessons.title: Working with APIs
lessons.content: APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) let your app communicate with servers to get or send data. REST APIs use HTTP methods: GET (retrieve data), POST (send data), PUT (update), DELETE (remove). Data is usually in JSON format. Making an API call: send a request with the URL and any needed parameters, wait for the response, parse the JSON into objects your app can use. Handle errors: no internet, server down, invalid data. Show loading states while waiting. Cache responses so the app works when offline.
examples: GET https://api.weather.com/current?city=Kampala — returns weather data as JSON
POST to a login endpoint with {email, password} — returns an auth token
Parse JSON: {'name': 'Alice', 'score': 95} → create a Student object in your app

keyTerms.API: Application Programming Interface — a way for apps to communicate with servers
keyTerms.REST: A common API style using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
keyTerms.JSON: JavaScript Object Notation — the standard format for sending structured data

quiz.question: What HTTP method retrieves data?
quiz.explanation: GET requests data from a server without modifying anything.

quiz.question: What format is API data usually sent in?
quiz.explanation: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard data format for APIs.

quiz.question: Why cache API responses?
options: So the app works when offline
quiz.explanation: Caching saves data locally so users can access it without an internet connection.

lessons.title: Testing Your App
lessons.content: Testing ensures your app works correctly before users see it. Unit tests check individual functions: does calculateTotal(10, 5) return 15? Widget tests verify UI components render correctly and respond to input. Integration tests check entire flows: can a user sign up, log in, and create a post? Test on real devices — emulators miss touch and performance issues. Test edge cases: empty input, no internet, very long text, rapid button tapping. Beta testing gives the app to real users before launch to find bugs you missed.
examples: Unit test: expect(add(2, 3), equals(5)) — verifies the add function works
Widget test: tap a button and verify a dialog appears
Beta test: give 20 users the app for a week and collect feedback on crashes and usability

keyTerms.unit test: Testing a single function or method in isolation
keyTerms.integration test: Testing complete user flows across multiple screens
keyTerms.beta testing: Giving pre-release app to real users to find bugs and get feedback

quiz.question: What does a unit test check?
quiz.explanation: Unit tests verify individual functions or methods produce expected results.

quiz.question: Why test on real devices?
options: Emulators miss touch and performance issues
quiz.explanation: Real devices show actual performance, touch response, and device-specific bugs.

quiz.question: What is beta testing?
options: Giving pre-release to real users for feedback
quiz.explanation: Beta testing lets real users find bugs and usability issues before public launch.

lessons.title: App Store Publishing
lessons.content: To publish on Google Play Store: create a developer account ($25 one-time fee), prepare app assets (icon, screenshots, description), build a signed release APK or App Bundle, fill in the store listing (title, description, category, privacy policy), and submit for review. The review takes hours to a few days. For Apple App Store: need an Apple Developer account ($99/year) and a Mac to build. Keep your app updated: fix bugs, add features, respond to user reviews. Follow store guidelines — apps can be rejected for policy violations (misleading content, privacy issues, crashes).
examples: Google Play requires: 512x512 app icon, at least 2 screenshots, a short and full description
Version numbering: 1.0.0 (first release), 1.1.0 (new features), 1.0.1 (bug fix)
A privacy policy is required — explain what data you collect and how you use it

keyTerms.APK: Android Package — the file format for installing Android apps
keyTerms.App Bundle: Modern Android format that optimizes delivery for each device
keyTerms.store listing: The page on the app store with screenshots, description, and reviews

quiz.question: How much does a Google Play developer account cost?
quiz.explanation: Google Play charges a one-time $25 fee for a developer account.

quiz.question: What is an App Bundle?
options: An optimized Android format that delivers only what each device needs
quiz.explanation: App Bundles let Google Play generate optimized APKs for each device configuration.

quiz.question: What do you need for iOS publishing?
options: Apple Developer account and a Mac
quiz.explanation: iOS apps must be built on a Mac with Xcode, and published through an Apple Developer account.

lessons.title: App Maintenance and Updates
lessons.content: Publishing is not the end — apps need ongoing maintenance. Monitor crashes using tools like Firebase Crashlytics — they show where and why the app crashes for users. Read user reviews and respond to feedback. Fix bugs promptly — a crashing app loses users fast. Plan regular updates: performance improvements, new features, OS compatibility (new Android/iOS versions may break things). Use analytics to understand how users actually use the app — which features are popular, where users drop off. A/B testing compares two versions of a feature to see which performs better.
examples: Firebase Crashlytics shows: 50 users crashed on the login screen — a null pointer on line 42
Analytics reveal: 80% of users never open Settings — move important options elsewhere
A/B test: version A has a blue button, version B has green — B gets 15% more clicks

keyTerms.crash reporting: Tools that automatically log and report app crashes with details
keyTerms.analytics: Tracking how users interact with the app to make data-driven decisions
keyTerms.A/B testing: Comparing two versions of a feature to see which performs better

quiz.question: Why monitor crash reports?
options: To find and fix bugs users are experiencing
quiz.explanation: Crash reports show exactly where the app fails so you can fix it quickly.

quiz.question: What is A/B testing?
options: Comparing two versions to see which performs better
quiz.explanation: A/B testing shows different versions to different users and measures which works better.

quiz.question: Why keep updating an app after launch?
options: Fix bugs, add features, stay compatible with new OS versions
quiz.explanation: Ongoing updates fix issues, add value, and ensure compatibility with device updates.
